brand.title: IQVIA (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to Social Selling Techniques

questions.question: What are the two axes that form the foundation of the Social Style Selling framework?
choices: Introversion vs. Extroversion and Logic vs. Emotion
Ask vs. Tell and Task vs. People
Speed vs. Accuracy and Data vs. Relationships
Control vs. Collaboration and Vision vs. Results
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the two axes are Ask vs. Tell (how someone gets what they want) and Task vs. People (what drives their behavior).
questions.feedback_incorrect: The framework is simpler than personality psychology. It focuses on two observable behavioral axes: how someone communicates (Ask or Tell) and what they prioritize (Tasks or People).

questions.question: Which of the following is a signature question that a Driver buyer typically leads with?
choices: How does this work and how was it measured?
What are the results and what is the outcome?
Why this solution and why now?
Who else is using this and who is involved?
questions.feedback_correct: You've got it—Drivers ask "What?" because they are focused on results and outcomes.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each style has a distinct signature question. Drivers are results-focused, so they ask "What?" to get straight to outcomes. The other answers belong to Analyticals (How), Amiables (Why), and Expressives (Who).

questions.question: What is the primary pressure behavior of an Amiable buyer when something goes wrong in a sales conversation?
choices: Takes control of the meeting and drives toward a decision
Asks for more time and requests additional data
Goes quiet and withdraws from the conversation
Becomes argumentative and pushes back hard
questions.feedback_correct: That's right—when Amiables feel pressured, they withdraw quietly rather than confront the issue directly.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Amiables avoid conflict and rushed decisions, so when stressed they go quiet and pull back. Taking control is a Driver move, asking for more data is an Analytical move, and becoming argumentative is an Expressive move.

questions.question: An Analytical buyer is asking detailed methodical questions and showing low emotion while focused on accuracy. What single adjustment would best support this buyer's decision-making process?
choices: Share a few inspiring stories about other successful clients and keep the energy high
Move quickly to conclusions and outcomes to respect their time
Allow adequate time for evaluation and provide documented evidence throughout the process
Spend extra time building personal rapport before discussing any business details
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—Analyticals need rigor, evidence, and time to evaluate; rushing or skipping documentation will damage trust.
questions.feedback_incorrect: While Analyticals do appreciate efficiency, what matters most to them is that the process is thorough and backed by data. Rushing, personal storytelling, or excessive relationship-building first will feel sloppy to them.

questions.question: You are a naturally direct, task-focused Driver rep, and you notice your Amiable buyer has become quiet and is giving shorter answers. What does this signal mean?
choices: The buyer is not interested and you should move toward closing quickly
Your direct, fast-paced approach has created friction and the buyer is withdrawing
The buyer is an introvert and will never be comfortable with sales conversations
You need to add more data and evidence to convince the Amiable to move forward
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—that withdrawal is an early warning sign that your natural style has created discomfort; this is the moment to slow down and shift your approach.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A sudden drop in engagement and withdrawal are not signs of disinterest or personality type—they are signs of a style mismatch. Your directness may feel pushy to an Amiable who needs rapport and collaboration first.

questions.question: Why does the Social Style framework specifically focus on observed behavior rather than personality labels or psychological categories?
choices: Because personality tests are more expensive than behavioral observation
Because you can watch and respond to observable behavior in real time, making it immediately actionable in a sales conversation
Because personality labels are more accurate but harder for sales reps to remember
Because the course author prefers not to use psychology in training materials
questions.feedback_correct: That's the key insight—observable behavior is practical and real-time, which means you can adjust your approach during a live conversation without needing to psychoanalyze anyone.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The model uses observed behavior because it is practical and immediate, not because of cost or memory. You are watching how someone communicates, what they ask about, and how much emotion they show—cues you can pick up in the first five minutes.

questions.question: A buyer displays both methodical, data-driven questioning (Analytical trait) and a warm, relationship-conscious approach (Amiable trait). How would the framework explain this mixed behavior?
choices: The framework cannot explain mixed behavior—the buyer must be classified as one pure style only
The buyer is exhibiting pressure behavior and you should slow down your approach
The buyer likely has an Analytical primary style with an Amiable adjacent style softening the primary
The buyer is being deceptive and you should not trust their behavior
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—the adjacent style sits next to the primary on the grid and modifies how the primary style shows up in behavior; this explains why someone does not feel like a pure style.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Nobody is a pure style. Most people have a primary style and an adjacent style that softens or shapes it. An Analytical with Amiable adjacency will still be methodical and data-focused, but more relationship-conscious than a pure Analytical.

questions.question: You are preparing for a meeting with an Expressive buyer. Based on the style-matched selling tactics, which approach will build rapport and keep them engaged?
choices: Front-load a detailed 30-slide deck with comprehensive data and product specifications
Spend discovery time asking about their vision and ambitions, show genuine enthusiasm, and involve them in talking about who else should be part of the solution
Lead with conclusions and results, keep the meeting brief, and offer three clear options to choose from
Build personal rapport for 20 minutes before discussing business, then ask detailed logical questions
questions.feedback_correct: You've nailed it—Expressives need to be heard, want to talk about vision and big possibilities, and will disengage from detail-heavy presentations.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Expressives are high-emotion, high-talk buyers focused on vision and people. A long data deck will lose them fast. They want to be engaged in conversation about possibilities and involvement, and they respond to your genuine enthusiasm.

questions.question: What is the most important single habit that defines versatility in the Social Style Selling framework?
choices: Developing a completely different personality for each of the four buyer styles
Building strong personal relationships with every buyer before attempting to sell anything
Reading observable cues, naming the style, and deliberately adjusting your communication approach accordingly
Identifying your own style and only selling to buyers who share the same style as you
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly right—versatility is a discipline based on one habit: observe, identify, adjust. You do not need to change who you are; you change how you communicate.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Versatility is not about being someone you are not or only selling to similar buyers. It is the deliberate habit of reading cues, naming the style, and adjusting your approach to match the buyer so they feel understood.

questions.question: Early in a conversation with a prospect, you hear them ask "Why this solution, why now, why you?" rather than leading with results or process questions. Which style are they most likely to be, and what is your immediate next move?
choices: They are likely a Driver; move quickly to clear outcomes and actionable next steps
They are likely an Amiable; invest time in rapport and use "we" language to signal collaboration
They are likely an Expressive; spend discovery time on their vision and use curiosity questions to let them elaborate
They are likely an Analytical; provide detailed evidence and allow time for evaluation
questions.feedback_correct: You caught the signature question—"Why?" is the Amiable's question because it signals their focus on relationships, fit, and purpose; rapport and collaboration language are your next move.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Each style has a signature question, and "Why?" belongs to the Amiable, who is focused on relationships and making sure the fit makes sense. Drivers ask "What?", Analyticals ask "How?", and Expressives ask "Who?"
